reasoning: Preserved all failure-driven edits as the higher-priority corrective guidance, including the expanded theorem-scope, equivalence, formula, algorithm-bound, constructive-claim, and asymptotic checks. Added the success-driven insights because they address distinct cases not directly covered by those edits; the endpoint-exponent note supplements rather than duplicates the general requirement to verify exact quantitative claims. No edits target the protected section.

edits.target: ## Match theorem claims to the exact setup
edits.content: - Use a proof-first comparison: establish the exact conclusion guaranteed under the stated hypotheses before ranking candidate claims. For an option framed as “strongest” or “complete,” split its base claim from every added clause and verify each one. A sharper estimate, stronger property, numerical lower bound, or explicit threshold is not validated merely because it sounds strongest; check the exact constants, factors, threshold, and parameter range. A known weaker conclusion does not justify upgrading to a stronger one. An existence result alone does not establish an asymptotic coefficient, sign, or long-time claim, and listing permitted parameter values does not show that every value occurs. A quantitative threshold is preferable to a vague eventual claim only when that threshold is actually established.

- Do not transfer a conclusion across regimes, object classes, or theorem formulations without checking scope. Match the exact equation or operator, solution notion, data regularity, parameter range, and, where relevant, the base theory and principle or domain. Existence alone does not establish a particular construction or uniqueness; conversely, nonuniqueness or uncertainty in a broad weak-solution class does not refute uniqueness in a specifically defined restricted class. For weak or distributional PDEs, justify regularity transfers and any integration by parts. In reverse mathematics, an equivalence over a different base theory or involving a different principle class or domain does not establish the stated equivalence.

edits.target: - For algorithm bounds, distinguish a fixed-parameter form f(k)n^c from n^{O(k)}: polynomial time for each fixed k alone does not establish FPT.
edits.content: - For algorithm bounds, distinguish a fixed-parameter form f(k)n^c from n^{O(k)}: polynomial time for each fixed k alone does not establish FPT. Conversely, an XP upper bound does not establish that no FPT algorithm exists, and it should not replace a stronger FPT guarantee when the applicable theorem provides one. Match the actual runtime bound before assigning a parameterized-complexity classification.

edits.target: - For an equivalence, check both implications.
edits.content: - For an equivalence, check both implications under all stated hypotheses. Do not reject an apparently stronger statement merely because the generic implication is one-way; the restricted class may force equivalence. Normalize competing formulations pairwise: different terminology or a structural reformulation may express the same condition, so do not choose based on which sounds more canonical. Use the definitions and exact theorem criterion to distinguish the options, or recognize when they are equivalent. Conditions already assumed in the stem are redundant and cannot distinguish the options.

edits.target: - For competing formulas, compare signs, coefficients, factors, index ranges, and wording such as “only one” versus “at most one.” Use definitions to check which terms and indices should appear; when useful, test a low-dimensional case, specialization, or boundary case rather than relying on plausibility.
edits.content: - For competing formulas, compare signs, coefficients, factors, index ranges, and wording such as “only one” versus “at most one.” Use definitions to check which terms and indices should appear; when useful, test a low-dimensional case, specialization, or boundary case rather than relying on plausibility. Do not infer an unfamiliar object's definition from its notation or a guessed application area; use the supplied definition or presentation, or a reliably identified theorem. If choices differ by congruences, reduce and compare them exactly. For divisibility, read the direction literally: “a divides b” means b is an integer multiple of a. Derive which quantity must be a multiple from the relevant transformation or invariant; a factor such as 2 in an operation's wording does not by itself determine the direction. For a universally quantified candidate inequality, use the stated maximum over vertices or edges and prove it for the full class or give a valid counterexample: passing a few test cases does not establish universality, and failure at one index does not refute a bound on a maximum.

edits.target: - Separate a claimed conclusion from an offered explanation: a correct conclusion does not by itself establish the proposed mechanism. Once a direct check distinguishes the options, commit rather than adding speculative exceptions.
edits.content: - Keep abstract and constructive claims distinct: an explicitly exhibited compatible metric implies metrizability, but metrizability alone does not supply an explicit construction. Likewise, a bound on total leftover does not establish exact coverage of a named component or specify where the leftovers occur; verify each such add-on directly.

edits.target: - Preserve the exact form of asymptotic assertions: note cutoffs, the order of iterated limits, and whether the claim uses a limit or limsup. Do not silently replace a truncated approximation with convergence to a full series.
edits.content: - When comparing asymptotic formulations, expand them into quantifiers or define a scalar error profile and derive the implications between claims. Do not assume an iterated limit, a limit superior, or an “for every tolerance, there exists a cutoff” formulation is stronger or weaker without checking what each requires for fixed and varying cutoffs.

- In a probabilistic classification, distinguish “the limit almost surely belongs to this finite list” from “each listed limit occurs with positive probability.” Treat per-index probability claims and joint claims, such as eventual residence in a region together with convergence, as separate assertions requiring support.

- When a claim requires strict local inequalities on a sequence with flat regions, inspect triples wholly within plateaus as well as those at their endpoints. A global trapezoidal or unimodal shape does not imply strictness at every index.

- A lower bound on a liminf growth exponent need not imply a uniform lower bound with a fixed constant at that exact exponent; subpolynomial losses may remain. Check the endpoint strength of the stated conclusion.

- To test an invariance claim, determine how the defining data transform and whether the proposed quantity remains unchanged under the relevant equivalences. Dimension counts alone do not establish or refute invariance.
